claims.text: The integrity of the native iron oxide film controls the onset of corrosion in Q235 steel under harsh chloride-rich conditions.
At room temperature, an intact native oxide layer acts as a passivating barrier against water and chloride ions.
Slight thickening of the native oxide layer improves its passivating-barrier function at room temperature.
Elevated temperature generates thermal stresses that cause microcracking of the oxide film.
Microcracking permits accelerated ingress of corrosive species and initiates localized degradation.
Controlled thermal oxidation can thicken or enhance the oxide layer on Q235 steel.
A continuous oxide layer restricts diffusion of corrosive species into the steel.
Restricted transport of corrosive species limits localized electrochemical reactions.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between the oxide and substrate induces stress and defects in the oxide at elevated temperature.
Oxide-film defects compromise barrier properties and facilitate accelerated localized corrosion.
At room temperature, Q235 steel with an intact or enhanced oxide film will have a lower corrosion rate than oxide-removed steel.
At approximately 80°C, samples with an initially protective oxide film will develop microcracks.
At elevated temperature, oxide microcracking will produce a marked increase in corrosion rate relative to the untreated reference.
A thicker initial oxide film may delay the onset of elevated-temperature corrosion.
Oxide-film integrity is expected to be a dominant corrosion-control mechanism under chloride-rich, moderate-to-high-humidity conditions.
Oxide-film integrity is expected to be less influential when mechanical wear, very low humidity, or other corrosive agents dominate degradation.

contradictions.description: The intervention describes chemical oxide removal as simulating a 'damaged/passivated state.' Under the stated mechanism, oxide removal represents a damaged or depassivated state, whereas passivation is attributed to an intact oxide film.
